paragraphs: Rav Huna, exilarch of Babylonia in Rabbi’s time. He descended through the males from Judah’s kings, from Jehoiachin—and from Zerubbabel, Yuchasin, in the order of the generations under Shemayah and Avtalyon—whereas Rabbi, who descended from Hillel, descended from Judah on his mother’s side. In Bereshit Rabbah, chapter 33, Rabbi said: “If Rav Huna the exilarch comes up here, I shall seat him above me, for he is from Judah and I am from Benjamin; he is from the males, and I from the females” (see above, Hillel the Elder and Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi). In Yuchasin, in the name of Rav Sherira Gaon: “In Rabbi’s days Rav Huna was exilarch in Babylonia. This is what we say in Horayot 11: Rabbi asked Rabbi Chiyya, ‘What of someone such as I—am I liable for a goat?’ He answered, ‘Your rival is in Babylonia.’ Who was that? Rav Huna”—the words “Who was that? Rav Huna” are absent in the Gemara—“and those in Babylonia are superior, being called ‘scepter.’ He died in Babylonia during Rabbi’s lifetime and was buried in the Land of Israel.” In the Jerusalem Talmud, Kilayim chapter 9, halakhah 4, they buried him beside Rabbi Chiyya. See above, Rav Huna the Babylonian; L.A. [ל״ע, unresolved], and this requires examination; see there what is written there. Once Rabbi Chiyya the Great entered before Rabbi and said, “Rav Huna is outside.” Rabbi’s face changed color. He said to him, “His coffin has come.” Shalshelet HaKabbalah, folio 32: “In Rav’s days”—it should read Rabbi’s—“there was Rav Huna, of David’s seed on his father’s side …; he died in year 4050.” End of quotation. But Dorot Olam writes that Rabbi Huna the Babylonian died in year 4050 (see above, Rav Huna), whereas Rav Huna the exilarch died during Rabbi’s lifetime, as above, and Rabbi died before the completion of the fourth millennium. Thus Shalshelet HaKabbalah is confused in its view. In Ruth Rabbah, on “Where you die, I shall die,” Rav Huna the exilarch asked Rav Chasdai, “What is the meaning of the verse ‘Remove the turban and lift off the crown’?” He answered …; he said to him, “You are kindness, and your words are kindness.” In the Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 7a, Rav Huna the Babylonian said to him, “Chisda is your name, and your words are gracious.” From this it would appear that Rav Huna the Babylonian, whose student Rav Chisda was, was also called exilarch. However, see Gittin there; this is its wording: the exilarch said to Rav Huna, “From where do we know that a crown is forbidden?” He answered, “From the rabbis, for we learned, ‘In the war ….’” Meanwhile Rav Huna rose to relieve himself. Rav Chisda said to him, “A verse is written: ‘Remove the turban ….’” Meanwhile Rav Huna came back …. He said, “By God, it is from the rabbis! But Chisda is your name ….” Rashi explains: Rav Chisda was Rav Huna’s student and would not answer in his presence; when Rav Huna rose, Rav Chisda said to the exilarch, “A verse is written.” See the Jerusalem Talmud, end of Sotah: the exilarch sent to Rav Chisda, “What is the meaning of the verse ‘Remove …’?” He answered, “The turban was removed; the crown was lifted off.” Rabbi Yochanan heard and said, “He is kindness, and his words are kindness.” End of quotation. Thus, according to the readings of the Gemara and the Jerusalem Talmud, Rav Huna the Babylonian is not called exilarch, and the reading in Midrash Ruth is erroneous. Rashi in Moed Katan requires examination. See Rabbah, son of Rav Huna. After the first Rav Huna, Mar Ukva was appointed in Babylonia (Yuchasin, in the name of Rav Sherira Gaon).
